strengths: Compelling and well-motivated problem formulation: Current time-series LLMs typically ingest static, full-sequence representations, which causes noise accumulation and computational inefficiency on long horizons. Formulating time-series reasoning as an active segment acquisition and sequential decision process is a fresh and practical perspective.

Well-designed collaborative self-play and training framework: Decoupling 'where to look' (controller) from 'how to reason' (reasoner) within a single policy model using role-based prompting is elegant. The hierarchical policy optimization, coupled with the reliability reward (estimating segment sufficiency via repeated reasoner sampling) and variance-guided sampling, directly addresses the diffuse credit assignment problem in tool-use/information-retrieval reasoning traces.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Evaluated across six diverse time-series reasoning benchmarks (clinical, nature, web, finance), consistently outperforming strong baselines (general LLMs, multimodal TS-LLMs, and vision-based reasoning models).

Thorough ablation and diagnostic analyses: The ablation study clearly substantiates each design choice (e.g., removing the reliability reward drops performance by over 21%). Additional analyses on input length scalability (up to 12k points), data utilization percentages, and alignment with time-series explainability (XAI) ground truth masks provide valuable insights.
weaknesses: Restriction to univariate settings: The formulation and all benchmark evaluations are restricted to univariate time series (e.g., reducing multi-lead ECGs to a single lead). In many real-world diagnostic or industrial scenarios, cross-variable interactions are critical, leaving the framework's behavior in multivariate settings untested.

Clarity on the controller's initial input encoding: In Section 4 and Appendix F (Example 5), the controller receives the 'full time series embedding' to select initial segments. It is somewhat ambiguous how the patch-based MLP encodes arbitrarily long sequences (e.g., up to 12k timesteps in Appendix J) without incurring quadratic attention overhead or resolution downsampling, and whether this full embedding leaks information that trivializes segment boundary prediction.

High training overhead: The nested rollout RL procedure (G=6 controller trajectories, each resampled N=6 times by the reasoner) introduces non-trivial computational overhead during post-training, requiring ~100 GPU-hours on 4x H100s for modest-sized training sets.

Relatively small test splits: As shown in Table 4, several benchmark test splits contain only ~200 examples (e.g., TRQA, ETI, ECG QA). While averaging over 8 runs helps reduce evaluation variance, larger test sets would provide stronger statistical guarantees for the reported performance gains.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated formulation: treating long, heterogeneous time series as an active resource to query dynamically via segment selection addresses a key bottleneck of static whole-sequence encoding in multimodal LLMs.

Well-designed hierarchical RL framework: decomposing the process into a Controller (for where to look) and a Reasoner (for how to reason) within a single policy model, coupled with a reliability-based reward from nested rollouts, effectively mitigates credit assignment and stochastic answer noise.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: evaluated across six diverse benchmarks spanning clinical, nature, and general domains, consistently outperforming text LLMs, time-series foundation models (e.g., ITFormer, OpenTSLM), and vision-language baselines.

In-depth ablations and analyses: the paper includes rigorous ablation of each system component (reliability reward, trajectory vs. myopic objective, variance-guided sampling), scaling experiments on long sequences, and comparisons with time-series explainability baselines (TimeX, TimeX++).
weaknesses: Restriction to univariate time series: while the mathematical formulation theoretically accommodates multivariate data, all empirical evaluations and segment selection mechanisms are confined to the univariate setting ($V = 1$), leaving real-world multi-channel applications (e.g., full 12-lead ECG) untested.

Inference and training overhead: the interactive controller-reasoner loop introduces multi-turn sequential generation overhead during inference (up to $2\times$ latency compared to single-pass baselines in Table 8) and substantial RL compute costs during post-training (~100 GPU-hours per dataset).

Heavy reliance on synthetic teacher supervision for SFT: the bootstrapping phase relies on structured traces generated by prompting GPT-5 with rendered plots and heuristic constraints (e.g., at most 3 segments, minimum length of 8), which may introduce inductive biases or limit generalization beyond the templated structure.
Minor presentation omissions: placeholder URLs for the project website and code in footnote 1 are empty, and some bibliographic entries (e.g., Jing et al.) are missing conference/year details.

strengths: Compelling and novel problem formulation: Framing time-series reasoning as an active, sequential decision problem—where the model iteratively selects informative segments rather than relying on a static, full-sequence encoding—addresses a key limitation in current time-series LLMs (e.g., context dilution and noise from irrelevant intervals).

Principled hierarchical collaborative self-play framework: The decoupling of 'where to look' (high-level controller) from 'how to reason' (low-level reasoner) using a single underlying policy model is elegant. In particular, utilizing a reliability reward (consistency across repeated reasoner rollouts) provides an effective supervision signal for segment selection in the absence of ground-truth segment annotations.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The approach is validated across six diverse benchmarks spanning clinical, nature, web, and synthetic domains, consistently outperforming standard LLMs, dedicated time-series encoder-LLMs, and vision-language approaches.

Thorough ablation studies and detailed appendices: The paper provides insightful analyses including data utilization curves (showing optimal performance around 30–70% sequence usage), sequence length scaling up to 12,000 steps, inference latency measurements, comparisons with time-series explainability methods (TimeX/TimeX++), and vision-based modality transfer.
weaknesses: Restriction to univariate time series: The method and evaluations are currently restricted to univariate signals (V = 1). Many critical real-world temporal reasoning applications (e.g., full 12-lead ECG analysis, multi-sensor ICU monitoring, multivariate financial indicators) require reasoning across multiple concurrent channels, where segment selection involves both temporal bounds and channel subsets.

Controller input paradox: As shown in the Controller Prompt (Appendix F, Example 5) and Section 3.3, the controller receives the full time series embedding at each step. While the reasoner benefits from conditioned, localized segments, having the controller process the full sequence embedding somewhat weakens the claim of avoiding full sequence consumption, and may still suffer from representation bottlenecks on extremely long sequences.

Computational overhead and sample complexity: The hierarchical RL optimization requires nested rollouts (G = 6 interaction rollouts, each with N = 6 reasoner rollouts, resulting in substantial rollouts per training step) and multi-turn iterative inference. Table 5 and Table 8 illustrate that training and inference costs are noticeably higher than single-pass fine-tuned baselines.

Reliance on proprietary models for SFT data generation: The SFT traces are generated by prompting GPT-5 with rendered visualizations and explicit constraints. The paper does not thoroughly analyze how dependent the framework is on the quality of GPT-5's initial reasoning traces or potential teacher-model artifacts.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated formulation: Treating time-series reasoning as an active, sequential segment-selection problem rather than relying on static, whole-sequence encodings addresses a critical bottleneck (attention dilution and irrelevant context in long sequences).

Principled post-training RL design: The collaborative self-play formulation cleanly decouples segment acquisition (controller) from answer reasoning (reasoner). The use of trajectory-level credit assignment, variance-guided rollout sampling, and a reliability reward (measuring reasoning consistency over repeated rollouts) is sound and technically well-executed.

Strong and comprehensive empirical results: ARTIST consistently outperforms seven competitive baselines across six diverse benchmarks (clinical, nature, and general domains). The analysis of time-series data utilization (Figure 3) provides compelling evidence that selective segment inspection improves reasoning accuracy over full-sequence consumption.

Thorough ablations: The ablation study clearly validates each core component, notably demonstrating the vital role of the reliability reward (a 21.4% drop when removed) and joint controller-reasoner optimization over single-role optimization.
weaknesses: Clarification needed on controller input vs. full sequence processing claims: The paper emphasizes that ARTIST avoids 'requiring full time series consumption'. However, Section 3.3 and Prompt Example 5 indicate that the controller receives the full time series embedding (<TS_DATA>) at each interaction step. While the reasoner operates on selected segments to prevent context dilution, the controller still ingests representations of the full sequence. The text should clarify the exact computational and representation footprint of the controller versus the reasoner.

Lack of inference runtime and latency analysis: Sequential, multi-round interaction between controller and reasoner inherently adds latency and computational overhead at inference time. While acknowledged in the limitations, the manuscript lacks quantitative measurements (e.g., wall-clock latency, token generation counts, or FLOPs) comparing ARTIST to single-pass baselines.

Scope limited to univariate signals: Real-world time series reasoning (especially in clinical settings like 12-lead ECGs or multi-channel EEGs, which were reduced to single-lead/single-channel setups here) often requires cross-channel reasoning across multivariate signals. Demonstrating how segment selection scales to multi-variable settings remains an open question.

Bootstrapping dependency on closed proprietary models: The initial SFT stage relies heavily on structured CoT traces generated by prompting GPT-5 with rendered visualizations, making reproducibility somewhat dependent on access to proprietary models.

strengths: Novel formulation of time-series reasoning as an active, sequential decision process where a single policy model alternates between high-level segment selection (controller) and low-level reasoning (reasoner).

Well-designed reinforcement learning framework: decoupling evidence acquisition from answer generation, using a reliability reward (measuring answer consistency under repeated reasoner rollouts) to supervise the controller, and employing variance-guided sampling to optimize training efficiency.

Comprehensive empirical validation across six diverse benchmarks spanning clinical, financial, acoustic, and general domains, outperforming text-based LLMs, dedicated time-series models, and vision-language models by an average of 6.46 percentage points.

Thorough ablation study (Table 3) rigorously isolating the contribution of key components, demonstrating that the reliability reward (+21.44%), trajectory-level optimization (+12.28%), and joint controller-reasoner training (+8.94%) are crucial to performance.

Insightful analysis of time-series data utilization (Figure 3), revealing that inspecting 30–70% of informative segments yields superior reasoning performance compared to processing the entire sequence.
weaknesses: Conceptual tension regarding context processing: While the paper argues that processing the full sequence dilutes salient local structure, the Controller still receives the full time series embedding at every interaction round (Equation 3 and Appendix F, Example 5). Clarification on whether the controller receives a downsampled/coarsened embedding or the full raw resolution would clarify the efficiency and context-dilution trade-offs.

Evaluation on heavily subsampled test sets: As shown in Table 4, the evaluation test sets are restricted to approximately 200 examples per dataset (totaling ~1,239 test examples). While 8 independent runs are reported, the paper does not explain why the test sets were truncated from their original sizes, leaving potential selection bias unaddressed.

Coarse credit assignment across controller steps: In Equation 16, the controller advantage is applied uniformly to all tokens across all interaction rounds $i \in \{1, \dots, L^{(g)}\}$. While effective in practice, this simple Monte Carlo trajectory-level credit assignment does not explicitly distinguish between early necessary segment retrievals and redundant intermediate steps.

Inference latency: As noted in the limitations, the iterative interaction between the controller and reasoner across multiple steps introduces non-trivial inference overhead compared to single-pass static reasoning models, but no quantitative inference latency/FLOPs comparisons are provided.

strengths: Formulating time-series reasoning as an active, query-adaptive segment acquisition problem is a conceptually appealing alternative to static full-sequence encoding.
The collaborative self-play framing neatly decouples segment localization (controller) from step-by-step reasoning and answer extraction (reasoner) within a single unified policy model.

The reliability reward mechanism, which scores the controller based on consistency across multiple reasoner rollouts rather than a single stochastic outcome, is well-motivated and supported by ablation results.
The paper is clearly structured and accompanied by intuitive illustrations (Figures 1 and 2) that clearly convey the trajectory rollout and hierarchical policy optimization pipeline.
weaknesses: Core conceptual inconsistency: The central motivation of the paper is to avoid forcing models to process a fixed, full view of long time series to prevent noise dilution and reduce data consumption. However, as formalized in Equation 3 and shown in the Controller Prompt (Appendix F, Example 5), the controller receives the full time series embedding at every single interaction round. Thus, the model still consumes and encodes the entire sequence globally before any segment selection occurs.

Anomalous metric degradation on RCW: In Table 1, while ARTIST + RL improves RCW accuracy from 69.75% to 77.00%, the F1 score drops precipitously from 61.46% to exactly 50.00% (the exact score of a random guess / trivial majority predictor on this binary dataset). This strongly indicates policy collapse to a degenerate majority-class prediction under RL, which is not analyzed or discussed in the text.

Marginal RL gains over SFT on small test sets: The test splits across all six benchmarks are quite small (each containing only ~200 to 226 examples, Table 4). On datasets such as ETI (+1.91%), TSQA (+1.94%), and TRQA (+0.80%), the improvement of RL over SFT corresponds to only 2 to 4 correctly answered test instances. Given that SFT provides the vast majority of the improvement over baselines, the added complexity of hierarchical RL provides modest evidential gains.

Substantial gap behind vision-based baselines on clinical data: On Sleep-QA (Table 2), TimeMaster + RL achieves 72.55% accuracy, nearly doubling ARTIST + SFT + RL's accuracy of 36.63%. The paper does not adequately investigate why segment selection fails so significantly compared to visual rendering on multi-class physiological signals.

High computational footprint during training and inference: Sampling G=6 multi-round interaction rollouts followed by N=6 final-round reasoner rollouts (yielding dozens of forward/generation passes per prompt per step) makes post-training computationally demanding, and multi-turn tool calling introduces notable latency at inference time.
